mainText:
If you only remember one thing: A I just had its first big public vote, and it was about buildings, not models.

One. Voters reject data centers. On November third, about forty local ballot measures across ten states went to voters. Data center opponents won nearly all of them. The one exception was Harwood, North Dakota. In Ashville, Ohio, more than eighty one percent voted no on a data center deal. Gallup finds seventy one percent of adults oppose a data center near them. Your A I Collective newsletter says the objections were about water, power bills, and secret deals, not what the models do. Open A I is now promising to limit N D A s with officials and cover electricity costs. It also wants to say compute campuses. Why it matters: the public judges A I by what it can see, a building on its street.

Two. Google ships Gemini four Carbon. Per your Batch newsletter, Google's new frontier model tops a major independent intelligence index, edging Claude Opus five point five. Access is limited to select cybersecurity defenders. Pricing is two dollars in and ten dollars out per million tokens, introductory. It arrived about two weeks after Gemini four Argon. Why it matters: top models are converging on price and score, so efficiency becomes the edge.

Three. Anthropic goes public. Anthropic publicly filed its I P O prospectus on October twenty sixth. Coverage highlights strong revenue growth and a computing bill near nine hundred billion dollars. Why it matters: an A I lab on the public markets means more disclosure about the real cost of A I.

Four. Chips and export controls. This one is background, not new. In June, the U S Commerce Department extended chip license rules to any company headquartered in China, wherever it operates. That closed the overseas subsidiary loophole for Nvidia and A M D chips. Why it matters: the chip fight now shapes where A I gets built.

Five. Tech for good. The International Rescue Committee's Signpost A I assistant raised its pass rate from fifty two to seventy seven percent in testing, and staff worked about seventy percent faster. It still gets about one answer in four wrong, so humans check every response. An A I tutor on WhatsApp is on track to reach nearly one million Nigerian children by year end, at about twenty cents per child. Why it matters: A I helps aid work most when people stay in the loop.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker: Stephen Miller was named White House chief of staff after the midterm rout. And Andrew Ng, in The Batch, says LinkedIn data shows A I has created about two million jobs.

The thread today: people want a say in A I, and they're starting with the parts they can see. Have a good Saturday.
